Addition of air-nanobubble water to mitigate the inhibition of high salinity 
on co-production of hydrogen and methane from two-stage anaerobic 
digestion of food waste 
Tingting Hou , Jiamin Zhao , Zhongfang Lei , Kazuya Shimizu , Zhenya Zhang * 
Graduate School of Life and Environmental Sciences, University of Tsukuba, 1-1-1 Tennodai, Tsukuba, Ibaraki, 305-8572, Japan   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Handling editor: Zhen Leng  
Keywords: 
Food waste 
Air-nanobubble water 
Two-stage anaerobic digestion 
Hydrogen 
Methane 
High salinity 
A B S T R A C T   
Most previous studies have focused on the effects of salt on anaerobic digestion (AD) for hydrogen or methane 
production. However, the effects of salt on two-stage AD and the related approaches to mitigate the adverse 
effects of high salinity on hydrogen and/or methane production were seldom addressed. In this study, addition of 
Air-nanobubble water (Air-NBW) was adopted to mitigate the inhibition of high salinity on co-production of 
hydrogen and methane from two-stage AD of food waste (FW). In the Air-NBW added reactors with 0–30 g NaCl/ 
L, hydrogen yield was increased by 21–65% with the subsequent methane yield elevated by 14–43% when 
compared to the corresponding deionized water (DW) group. This study for the first time confirmed that when 
two-stage AD of FW was exposed to the same salinity level, addition of Air-NBW could enhance enzymatic ac­
tivities at the individual stage. Results of electron transport system (ETS) activity further demonstrate that 
addition of Air-NBW may promote the electron transfer associated with the synthesis of hydrogen and methane. 
Therefore, an efficient approach for hydrogen and methane recovery from the two-stage AD of FW under high 
salinity was proposed through improving microbial electron transfer and corresponding enzymatic activities at 
each stage via Air-NBW addition.   
1. Introduction 
Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has reported that about 1/ 
3 of the food produced globally is lost or wasted in agroindustry and 
households (FAO, 2013a,b). As known, food waste (FW) generated by 
household consumption (household preparation and cooking) accounts 
for a large part of the total FW production, which was estimated as 
7.7–10.14 million tonnes in Japan, with 94% being disposed by land­
filling or incineration (Liu et al., 2016). However, landfilling is consid­
ered the least environmentally friendly option (FAO, 2013a,b). Yano 
and Sakai (2016) reported that Japan has historically adopted inciner­
ation as the primary treatment method for FW due to the lack of land­
filling space, and currently the incinerator facilities are facing a 
seriously aging issue. In contrast, anaerobic digestion (AD) is considered 
an environmentally friendly technology for the management of FW 
because it can reduce negative impacts on the environment and recover 
bioenergy (H2 and CH4) and biofertilizers simultaneously. 
Generally, the salinity of FW is high because salt (NaCl) is one of the 
seasonings widely used in the cooking process (He et al., 2019). 
Particularly in Japan, the salt intake is higher (≥11 g per day) than in 
western societies according to the diverse eating habits (Kuwabara et al., 
2020), indicating its higher salt concentration feature in FW. Never­
theless, the high salinity could cause an inhibitory effect on microor­
ganisms’ growth due to the increased osmotic pressure or dehydration 
effect (Tsapekos et al., 2019). Many previous studies have investigated 
the inhibition of salt on AD processes, including hydrolysis, acido­
genesis, and methanogenesis. For instance, Lee et al. (2012) investigated 
the sodium inhibition on hydrogen production from a pure culture of 
C. butyricum, in which hydrogen production started to decrease at ≥2 g 
Na+/L and the critical Na + concentration for ceased H2 production was 
estimated as 32 g Na+/L. Also, a sharp decrease in methane yield was 
noticed when NaCl was > 8 g/L (Anwar et al., 2016). Restated, under 
high salinity conditions, the high osmotic pressure and inappropriate 
enzyme linkages may lead to plasmolysis and loss of cell activity, which 
are the main reasons for inhibited AD processes (Zhang et al., 2020). 
Microorganisms indeed play a key role in the success of AD systems, and 
their activities largely influence the performance of AD systems. Liu 
et al. (2019) reported about 20% and 57% inhibition on the

enhancement of microbial activity may be an appropriate strategy to 
mitigate salt inhibition on AD of high salinity FW. 
Up to the present, most studies mainly focused on the effects of salt 
on AD for hydrogen or methane production, and few studies have been 
conducted to improve the efficiency of AD under high salt concentra­
tions. Currently, few technologies are available to effectively mitigate 
the inhibition of high salinity on AD of FW, except for simple dilution 
with water or mixing with other low-salt organic wastes. Liu et al. 
(2019) attempted to ameliorate salt inhibition on methane production 
from the kitchen waste AD system by adding osmoprotectant (glycine 
betaine (GB)), and 2.0 and 2.5 g/L GB were found to be the optimal 
dosages for 5 and 10 g Na+/L reactors with the resultant 29% and 62% 
increase in methane yield, respectively. However, the production cost of 
osmoprotectant is high, and a superfluous addition of osmoprotectant 
may adversely affect methane production. 
Nanobubble water (NBW), containing tiny bubbles with a diameter 
< 1000 nm, has been reported to enhance the activities of microor­
ganisms under both anaerobic and aerobic conditions for wastewater 
treatment (Agarwal et al., 2011; Temesgen et al., 2017). Additionally, 
NBW has been specifically applied to enhance the bioactivities of en­
zymes involved in AD systems of various organic wastes. For instance, 
Yang et al. (2019) and Wang et al. (2020a) found that addition of N2- 
and O2-NBW enhanced hydrolase activities in the AD of waste activated 
sludge and cellulase activity and electron transport system (ETS) activity 
in the AD of cellulose. Most recently, addition of Air-NBW was observed 
to not only enhance the hydrolase activities at the end of the hydro­
lysis/acidification stage but also improve the coenzyme F420 activity at 
the end of the methanogenesis stage in the two-stage AD of FW (Hou 
et al., 2021). However, the effects of NBW on microbial activities under 
high salinity conditions have not been determined. In addition, it is 
generally required to premix with some dilution water in a wet AD 
system to evenly distribute intermediate metabolites and microorgan­
isms in the whole reactor. Besides, high total solids (TS) would lead to 
the accumulation of more toxic substances like free ammonia nitrogen, 
especially in the AD systems of FW, which may require water addition to 
adjust TS concentration appropriately (Wang et al., 2020b; Zhou et al., 
2019). As such, NBW as a zero-pollution strategy may be considered as 
alternative water in the wet two-stage AD of FW, achieving enhanced 
microbial activity and thus mitigating salt inhibition on AD. 
This study for the first time investigated the response behaviors of 
hydrogen and methane co-production from the two-stage AD of FW 
under different salt concentrations. Then, the effects of Air-NBW intro­
duction on mitigating high salinity inhibition on AD of FW were eval­
uated by analyzing the variations of volatile fatty acids (VFAs), proteins, 
and carbohydrates. Ultimately, underlying mechanisms were pre­
liminary explored by monitoring the enzymatic activities and ETS ac­
tivity under Air-NBW addition at different salt concentrations. This 
study may provide an insight into the mechanisms involved in the two- 
stage AD of high salinity FW, targeting highly efficient energy recovery 
and sustainable management of FW. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. FW, inoculum and Air-NBW 
According to Liu et al. (2017) and He et al. (2019), the simulated FW 
was comprised of rice (25%), noodle (22%), pork (16%), cabbage (29%), 
and tofu (8%). Before starting the experiments, the FW was smashed and 
homogenized into slurries using a food grinder and stored at −20◦C. 
Inoculum applied in this study was anaerobically digested sludge 
sampled from the anaerobic digester of a wastewater treatment plant in 
Tsuchiura, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan. The physicochemical characteris­
tics of the FW and inoculum are summarized in Table 1. 
Air-NBW was selected in this study, which was generated according 
to the procedures provided by Wang et al. (2019) and Yang et al. (2019). 
The gas-water circulation method was adopted by using a NBW gener­
ator (HACK FB11, Japan), with the pressure and the flow rates of gas and 
water being controlled at 0.22 – 0.25 MPa, 0.05 L/min, and 3 L/min for 
20 min. Air used for the Air-NBW generation was taken directly from the 
natural environment of the laboratory. 
2.2. Effects of Air-NBW addition on the two-stage AD of FW at different 
salt concentrations 
2.2.1. Hydrogen production (the first stage of AD) 
All experiments of both stages were performed in the closed Schott 
Duran serum bottles of 250 mL with an effective volume of 150 mL each. 
In the first stage, according to the volatile solids (VS) content of FW and 
inoculum in Table 1, 6.5 g raw FW (wet weight) and 70 g inoculum were 
added to each reactor at a substrate to inoculum ratio (S/I) of 4:1 (VS 
basis). Then each bottle was diluted to the effective volume with 
deionized water (DW) or Air-NBW. As a result, the initial total VS was 
12.76 ± 0.17 g/L. Afterwards, different amounts of salt (NaCl) were 
added to these reactors to obtain the pre-designed NaCl concentrations 
of 0, 5, 10, 20, and 30 g/L, respectively. At this stage, the initial pH was 
adjusted to the optimal pH (5.50 ± 0.20) considering the activity of 
hydrogenase. The reactors were denoted as FW + DW-0, FW + DW-5, 
FW + DW-10, FW + DW-20, and FW + DW-30 when DW was applied at 
salt concentrations of 0, 5, 10, 20, and 30 g/L, respectively. Similarly, 
the reactors were labelled as FW + Air-NBW-0, FW + Air-NBW-5, FW +
Air-NBW-10, FW + Air-NBW-20, and FW + Air-NBW-30, respectively 
when Air-NBW was supplemented. 
2.2.2. Methane production (the second stage of AD) 
In the second stage, anaerobically digested sludge was firstly acti­
vated for about two weeks under 38 ± 1◦C until no gas production, with 
TS and VS of 0.80 ± 0.01% and 0.55 ± 0.01%. 50 g remaining acidified 
slurry from the first stage was added as the substrate to each bottle 
together with 50 g activated inoculum (S/I = 2:1 (VS basis)) to produce 
methane. Then each bottle was diluted to the effective volume with DW 
or Air-NBW, resulting in an initial total VS of 6.01 ± 0.70 g/L with the 
initial pH being adjusted to 7.50 ± 0.10. Similarly, different amounts of 
NaCl were supplemented to each reactor to make the final NaCl con­
centrations to be 0, 5, 10, 20, or 30 g/L in the reactor with the same 
designations as in Section 2.2.1. 
Before starting the experiments, all the reactors were flushed with 
high purity nitrogen (purity ≥99.9995%) around 2 min for 3 times to 
remove oxygen and then placed in a thermostatic incubator at 38 ± 1◦C 
for 92 h in the first stage and 36 d in the second stage, respectively. 
2.3. Analytical methods 
2.3.1. General parameters and calculations 
According to the standard methods (APHA, 2012), TS was analyzed 
by drying the samples at 105 ± 1◦C till constant weight, and VS was 
recorded as the loss of dry mass after burning at 600 ± 2◦C for 3 h. All 
liquid samples were centrifuged at 9,900 rpm for 20 min to obtain the 
supernatant and then filtered through 0.45 μm membrane filters before 
being analyzed. The concentrations of soluble proteins and carbohy­
drates were quantified using Lowry’s method and Phenol-sulfuric acid

2.3.2. Microbial enzyme activities and ETS activity at each stage 
The inhibition on hydrogen or methane production from the AD of 
FW under high salinity to a great extent depends on its impacts on mi­
crobial activities (Chen et al., 2018). More specifically, the main func­
tional microorganisms in each stage are different in the two-stage AD 
process. Besides, the mechanisms involved in the influence of salinity on 
hydrolase activity in the first stage and coenzyme F420 in the second 
stage remain unclear. Therefore, it is necessary to evaluate the effect of 
high salinity on the major microbial enzyme activities and whether 
addition of Air-NBW could alleviate the inhibition of salt on microor­
ganisms. In this study, the activities of α-glucosidase and protease at the 
end of the first stage and coenzyme F420 at the end of the second stage 
were measured according to the methods as previously described (Hou 
et al., 2021). For the determination of α-glucosidase, 0.1% p-nitro­
phenyl-α-D-glucopyranoside was used as substrate: 1 mL sample and 1 
mL substrate were added in a 10 mL centrifuge tube, then 2 mL 
HAc-NaAc buffer (0.2 M, pH 7.5) was added to mix uniformly. After 
standing for 30 min at 55◦C, 4 mL Na2CO3 (0.4 M) was added to 
terminate the reaction, and the absorbance was measured at 410 nm. 
Besides, 1% casein was used as the substrate to determine the activity of 
protease: 1 mL sample and 1 mL substrate were firstly added in a 10 mL 
centrifuge tube which was then placed at 55◦C for 10 min. After 2 mL 
trichloroacetic acid (0.4 M) being added to terminate the reaction, 
centrifugation was performed and then filtered through 0.45 μm mem­
brane filter. In the second step, 1 mL filtrate, 5 mL Na2CO3 (0.4 M), and 1 
mL Folin-phenol were added successively, and the absorbance was 
measured at 640 nm after being placed at 40◦C for 20 min. 
In addition, the microbial activities during the hydrogen and 
methane production stages were assessed by monitoring the electron 
transport rate. The ETS activity was tested using the 2-(p-iodophenyl)-3- 
(p-nitrophenyl)-5-phenyltetrazolium chloride-electron transport system 
(INT-ETS) method, which has been described in detail previously (Wang 
et al., 2020a). 
2.4. Statistical analysis 
All the reactors operation were conducted in duplicate with the 
measurements being in triplicate. All the data were processed by 
Microsoft Excel (2010). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was 
conducted to analyze the statistical difference between the conditions 
with or without the Air-NBW addition in the two-stage AD of FW at 
different salt concentrations. Statistical significance was assumed at p <
0.05. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effect of Air-NBW addition on hydrogen production from the first 
stage AD of FW at different salt concentrations 
3.1.1. Hydrogen production rate and cumulative hydrogen yield 
As seen in Fig. 1 a, the peak values of average hourly hydrogen 
production occurred firstly in the salt-free digesters (FW + DW-0 and 
FW + Air-NBW-0). When salinity was ≥20 g NaCl/L, the peak values of 
average hourly hydrogen production decreased significantly with the 
increase of salinity under no and addition of Air-NBW (p = 2.27 × 10−5 
for the DW group and 1.63 × 10−6 for the Air-NBW group, both p ≪ 
0.05). This indicates that high salinity may inhibit hydrogen production, 
which is consistent with the negative effects of salt on hydrogen pro­
duction in previous studies. Kim et al. (2009) obtained 30%, 60%, and 
90% inhibition on hydrogen production at 2.41, 5.36, and 10.14 g 
Na+/L, respectively. Similarly, Zhang et al. (2017) observed that 
hydrogen production could be gradually decreased with the salinity 
increase, and the inhibitory effect was more obviously at salinity ≥15 g 
NaCl/L. It is noteworthy that the peak values of average hourly 
hydrogen production in the Air-NBW group were higher than those in 
the DW group under the test salinity conditions (0 – 30 g NaCl/L). 
The cumulative hydrogen yield showed similar trends (Fig. 1b) and 
the maximum hydrogen yield of 197.55 ± 0.63 mL/g-VSadded was ob­
tained from FW + Air-NBW-0, about 28% higher than that from FW +
DW-0. It is worth mentioning that FW + Air-NBW-5 (185.64 ± 2.53 mL/ 
g-VSadded) also obtained approximately 20% higher than FW + DW-0. 
Moreover, the cumulative hydrogen yields from the Air-NBW added 
reactors were increased by 30%, 21%, 65%, and 65% in comparison to 
the DW added reactors at 5, 10, 20, and 30 g NaCl/L, respectively. As 
seen, salt inhibition on hydrogen production was more obviously in the 
reactors with DW addition (Fig. 2a). This observation indicates that 
addition of Air-NBW can effectively ameliorate the inhibition of salt on 
hydrogen production from the two-stage AD of FW. As reported previ­
ously, the inhibition of high concentration salt on AD was mainly caused 
by the loss of microbial activity (Anwar et al., 2016). However, Air-NBW 
supplementation can significantly increase the hydrolase activity in the 
two-stage AD of FW, which may be the reason for the reduced inhibition 
of salt on hydrogen production under addition of Air-NBW. This would 
be further discussed in Section 3.1.3. 
The kinetic parameters were estimated as shown in Table 2. The 
maximum hydrogen production potential (PH2) and the maximum 
hydrogen production rate (RH2, max) were decreased with the increase of 
salt concentration, regardless of whether Air-NBW was added or not. 
However, the values for the reactors with Air-NBW addition were higher 
than those for the corresponding reactors with DW addition. Upon the 
increase in salt concentration, the lag time (λ) seemed to increase 
correspondingly. In contrast, Air-NBW group had about 23 – 42% 
shorter λ (λ = 6.00 – 14.64 h) in comparison to the DW group (λ = 10.33 
– 19.17 h). This observation implies that addition of Air-NBW can 
accelerate the start-up of the AD process even under salt inhibition 
conditions. 
3.1.2. Potential impact of salt on the hydrolysis/acidification upon Air- 
NBW addition

cation. Therefore, VFAs were monitored in the first stage as shown in 
Fig. 2b. A remarkably negative effect on VFAs production was noticed 
with the increase of salt concentrations (p = 1.19 × 10−6 for the DW 
group and p = 1.74 × 10−8 for the Air-NBW group, both p ≪ 0.05). It has 
been found that VFAs yield was inhibited at > 6 g NaCl/L, with the 
production being reduced at least by 44.8% at > 9 g NaCl/L (Liu et al., 
2017). Zhao et al. (2016) claimed that VFAs production was enhanced 
when salt concentration was < 8 g/L, while severely inhibited when the 
salt concentration was further increased. In this study, higher total VFAs 
productions were achieved from the Air-NBW added reactors, increasing 
by 6 – 18% when compared to the DW added ones. This observation is in 
agreement with that of hydrogen yield, probably due to the fact that acid 
production is usually accompanied by hydrogen production.

Regarding the changes of individual VFA concentration, a clear H2 
production through the HAc and HBu pathway was noticed in all the 
reactors. This indicates that the HBu-type fermentation was the main 
fermentation type in this study according to Lay (2000) and Zhang et al. 
(2017). However, at high salinity levels, HAc and HBu productions were 
reduced, which may be the main reason for the lower H2 yields in the 
high salinity reactors. 
Ginkel and Logan (2005) detected that a larger amount of the un­
dissociated HAc and HBu was present under lower pH conditions, which 
led to the inhibited H2 production. Additionally, the undissociated HBu 
may exert a more negative effect on H2 yield than the undissociated 
HAc. Table 3 summarizes the changes of final pH, undissociated HAc, 
and undissociated HBu concentrations in all the reactors. As shown, the 
concentrations of undissociated HAc and HBu were increased with the 
increase of salinity, while a lower increase was clearly noticed in the 
Air-NBW added reactors. Heuvel et al. (1992) claimed that the undis­
sociated acid at the critical inhibitory concentration (50 mM) may 
greatly increase the cell maintenance energy requirements and deplete 
the ATP reserves necessary for the metabolic switch to solventogenesis. 
In this study, addition of Air-NBW reduced the accumulation of undis­
sociated acid, which might be resulted from its enhancement effect on 
the microbial activity as discussed later. 
Soluble proteins and carbohydrates play a crucial role in microbial 
growth and hydrogen production by anaerobic fermentation (Laspidou 
and Rittmann, 2002). As shown in Fig. 3a and b, the initial concentra­
tions of soluble proteins and carbohydrates were 1014.15 ± 78.82 and 
2278.26 ± 128.12 mg/L in all the reactors. After the hydrogen pro­
duction stage, the concentrations of soluble proteins and carbohydrates 
declined remarkably in the reactors with lower salinity (0–10 g NaCl/L). 
However, higher concentrations of soluble proteins and carbohydrates 
were always detected in the reactors with higher salinity (≥20 g 
NaCl/L), especially in the DW added reactors. Zhao et al. (2017) 
revealed that the concentrations of soluble carbohydrates and proteins 
were increased from 8596 and 2156 mg COD/L to 12,054 and 3124 mg 
COD/L, respectively when NaCl was increased from 2 to 15 g/L in the 
AD system of FW. This observation suggests that high salinity may 
accelerate the release of proteins and carbohydrates due to the bacterial 
protective responses to high salinity stress (Wang et al., 2013). It was 
noted that the declines in soluble proteins and carbohydrates were more 
remarkable in the Air-NBW group: (1) they had about 14%, 21%, 48%, 
68%, and 113% higher declines in soluble proteins concentrations, and 
(2) about 11%, 16%, 7%, 13% and 14% higher declines in soluble 
carbohydrates concentrations than the reactors with DW addition when 
NaCl varied from 0 to 30 g/L. On the one hand, this phenomenon in­
dicates that the prolonged exposure of microorganisms to high salinity 
may lead to cell lysis or dissolution, reducing the hydrolysis of proteins 
and carbohydrates. On the other hand, it also suggests that addition of 
Air-NBW rather than DW may not only ameliorate the above negative 
effect but also promote the hydrolysis of organic matters under high 
salinity conditions. Wang et al. (2017) applied Scanning Electron Mi­
croscopy and observed more pores and channels on the surface of sludge 
after being treated with air micro-bubbles, which is conducive to the 
formation of zoogloea. 
3.1.3. Activities of ETS and extracellular hydrolases during the first stage 
AD of FW 
In this study, the microbial activity indicated by the electron trans­
port rate and extracellular hydrolases was monitored during the first 
stage. As illustrated in Fig. 3c, the ETS activity was detected to increase 
and then decrease along with the lower salt concentrations (≤10 g 
NaCl/L); however, in the DW added reactors with 20 and 30 g NaCl/L, a 
continuous decline of ETS activity was noticed. The highest ETS activity, 
71.78 mg/(g⋅h), was obtained at 44 h in FW + Air-NBW-0. At the end of 
the first stage, the ETS activities in the Air-NBW added reactors were 5 – 
92% higher than the DW added reactors at the test salt concentrations. 
This observation implies the enhanced electron transfer effect under the 
Air-NBW addition condition, and thus the increased bioactivity of mi­
crobes, which could be ascribed to the involvement of Air-NBs in elec­
tron transfer with resultant enhanced synthesis of hydrogen from their 
negatively charged surfaces. A detailed explanation is given in Section 
3.3. 
Fig. 3d displays the relative activities of α-glucosidase and protease 
in all the reactors at the end of the first stage with the extracellular 
hydrolases of FW + DW-0 being as the reference (100%). Clearly, high 
salinity may inhibit the activity of hydrolases to some extent when 
compared to the salt-free reactors. For instance, the relative activity of 
α-glucosidase was decreased by 13%, 15%, 24%, and 38% in FW + DW- 
5, FW + DW-10, FW + DW-20, and FW + DW-30, respectively. However, 
less inhibition was observed on the activity of protease when compared 
to that of α-glucosidase. For example, the relative activity of protease did 
not decrease but increased slightly by 2% at salt concentration of 5 g 
NaCl/L. And the relative activity of protease was decreased by 8%, 17%, 
and 29% in FW + DW-10, FW + DW-20, and FW + DW-30, respectively. 
Besides, it is worth noting that 9 – 20% higher α-glucosidase and 0.4 – 
22% increase in protease activities were detected in the Air-NBW added 
reactors than those in the DW added reactors at salt concentrations of 0 – 
30 g/L, reflecting the higher bioactivities of anaerobes in the former 
reactors. Therefore, supplementation of Air-NBW is regarded as an 
effective strategy to enhance microbial activities under high salinity, 
even for hydrogen production from the AD of FW. 
3.2. Effect of Air-NBW addition on methane production from the second 
stage AD of FW at different salt concentrations 
3.2.1. Methane production rate and cumulative methane yield 
In the second stage, the remaining hydrolyzed and acidified organic 
slurries at the end of the first stage were used as the substrates for 
methane production. Much attention was paid to the effect of salt on 
methane production from the second stage AD of FW with or without 
Air-NBW addition. The daily methane production as shown in Fig. 4a 
clearly indicates some prolongation effect of salt on the reactor start-up 
and progress. More specifically, when the salt concentration was 20 g 
NaCl/L (FW + DW-20), the peak daily methane production was reached 
on day 30, with 18 days later than FW + DW-0; furthermore, when the 
salt concentration was 30 g NaCl/L (FW + DW-30), the reactor failed to 
reach the peak daily methane production till the end of the experiment 
(day 36). There are some halophilic anaerobic microbial communities 
(Lefebvre et al., 2006), while these halophilic microorganisms are

high salinity FW, anaerobic microbes should be given enough time to

Regarding the cumulative methane yield (Fig. 4b), a significant 
reduction was observed at high salinity, especially in the DW added 
reactors. In the Air-NBW added reactors, the cumulative methane yields 
were increased by 19%, 16%, 20%, 14%, and 43% when compared to 
the DW added reactors at 0, 5, 10, 20, and 30 g NaCl/L, respectively. As 
seen from Fig. 4c, the inhibition degrees of methane production were 
8%, 14%, 34%, and 83% in FW + DW-5, FW + DW-10, FW + DW-20, 
and FW + DW-30, respectively. Compared with previous studies, the 
two-stage AD of high-salt FW in this study was more resistant to salt 
inhibition on methane production. For instance, Anwar et al. (2016) 
claimed that the inhibition degrees of one-stage kitchen waste AD sys­
tem were 24%, 33%, 56%, and 81% in the reactors at 10, 12, 14, and 16 
g NaCl/L, respectively. And 80% and 91% of inhibition degrees were 
obtained on methane production from the one-stage AD of FW at 10 and 
15 g NaCl/L, respectively (Zhao et al., 2017). Two-stage AD of FW used 
in this study may add some mitigation effect of salt inhibition on 
methane production because the microorganisms in the first stage have 
been exposed and got accommodated to the high salinity conditions. 
Additionally, it is interesting to notice that the methane yields from the 
Air-NBW added reactors at 0, 5, and 10 g NaCl/L were increased by 
about 19%, 7%, and 3% in comparison to that from FW + DW-0, and the 
inhibition degrees of methane production were only 26% and 76% in 
FW + Air-NBW-20 and FW + Air-NBW-30, respectively. These results 
imply that addition of Air-NBW could also effectively reduce the salt 
inhibition on methane production in the second stage AD of FW. 
3.2.2. Variations of organic matters concentration during the second stage 
AD 
The initial and final concentrations of soluble proteins and carbo­
hydrates in the second stage AD are displayed in Fig. 5a. The initial 
concentrations of soluble proteins in all the reactors were higher than 
those of soluble carbohydrates. It is probably because the hydrolysis of 
proteins in the first stage was not as sufficient as that of carbohydrates, 
resulting in more residual proteins. The hydrolysis of proteins has been 
reported later than that of carbohydrates and thus required a longer 
hydrolysis time (Kim et al., 2019), which was also verified in this study. 
Especially under high salt concentrations, the initial concentrations of 
soluble proteins and carbohydrates in the second stage were higher, 
which need to be further hydrolyzed in the second stage with a pro­
longed lag time. This could also be one of the reasons for the prolonged 
start-up of methane production with the increase of salt concentration. 
The VFAs produced in the first stage were the primary substrates that 
could be directly converted into methane by methanogens during the 
second stage. Therefore, a high initial VFAs concentration in the second 
stage is conducive to methane production (De Gioannis et al., 2017). As 
shown in Fig. 5b, higher initial VFAs concentrations were detected in the 
reactors with low salt concentrations (0 – 10 g NaCl/L), and addition of 
Air-NBW could produce more VFAs in the first stage, which can be 
utilized by methanogens in the second stage. However, when the salt 
concentration was 30 g NaCl/L, the total VFAs concentration was not 
decreased but increased at the end of the methane production stage, 
particularly in FW + DW-30. Due to the hydrogen production metabolic 
pathway, the first stage was dominated by HBu, which was followed by 
HAc with little propionic acid (HPr) production (the initial VFAs for the 
second stage). Nevertheless, HPr was accumulated, around 180 and 285 
mg/L in the FW + DW-20 and FW + DW-30 at the end of the second 
stage, respectively. HAc is regarded as the preferable substrate for 
methane production, while HPr is not conducive to the utilization by 
methanogens (Capson-Tojo et al., 2018). These data suggest that the 
inhibition of high salinity (≥20 g NaCl/L) on methanogenesis may be 
attributable to low efficiency of hydrolysis/acidification in the first stage

3.2.3. Activities of ETS and coenzyme F420 in the second stage AD of FW at 
different salt concentrations 
The ETS activities in the reactors with or without Air-NBW addition 
were assessed during the 36 days’ methanogenesis as shown in Fig. 5c. 
In the reactors with low salinity (0 – 10 g NaCl/L), the significant in­
crease in ETS activity was detected, especially in the Air-NBW added 
reactors. However, the ETS activities in FW + DW-20 and FW + DW-30 
were decreased slightly during the first 12 days, reflecting the negative 
effect of high salinity on ETS of microorganisms and thus reduced mi­
crobial activity. On the contrary, the ETS activities in the FW + Air- 
NBW-20 and FW + Air-NBW-30 were increased continually during the 
whole process, indicating that addition of Air-NBW was beneficial for 
mitigating the adverse effect of high salinity on ETS activity in the 
methanogenesis. At the end of the second stage, the ETS activity was 
increased by 9 – 30% in the Air-NBW added reactors when compared to 
the DW added reactors. In addition, after the 36 days’ methane pro­
duction, the relative activities of coenzyme F420 in all the reactors 
exhibited the same trend (Fig. 5d), i.e., when FW + DW-0 was taken as 
the reference (100%), the activity of coenzyme F420 was detected to 
remarkably decrease at high salinity levels, which were 73%, 62%, 54%, 
and 40% in the DW added reactors, and 130%, 110%, 99%, 72%, and 
49% in the Air-NBW added ones at 5, 10, 20, and 30 g NaCl/L, respec­
tively. These results indicate that addition of Air-NBW could enhance 
methane production by increasing microbial activity even under high 
salinity conditions. 
3.3. Preliminary analysis of mechanisms involved in this study 
Salt toxicity to microorganisms is predominantly determined by 
cations (Anwar et al., 2016), and the main cation in FW is Na+ because 
FW salinity mainly derives from food flavoring agents (NaCl). Osmotic 
pressure would increase sharply at high salt concentrations leading to 
plasmolysis and ultimately cell lysis and death (Fig. 6). This is why high 
salinity has a negative effect on AD. Meegoda et al. (2019) found that 
negatively charged NBs in an electrolyte solution (0.001 – 0.1 M NaCl) 
could combine with Na+ to form the electric double layer, which may 
prevent Na+ from entering the cell, thus reducing adverse effects of Na+
on microorganisms. However, the effect of high salinity on the 
morphology of NBs cannot be ignored. As reported by Das (2011) and 
Bunkin and Shkirin (2012), low salinity exerts an imperceptible effect on 
physicochemical characteristics of NBs, but when the NBs are exposed to 
a high salinity solution for a while, the bubble size, surface charge 
density, and the number of negative charges would increase. Never­
theless, the possible effect of these observations on AD is unclear. 
As shown in Fig. 6, during the H2 production stage, addition of Air- 
NBW enhanced the activities of ETS and extracellular hydrolases at 
different salt concentrations, which are likely attributable to the 
involvement of Air-NBs in the electron transfer associated with the 
synthesis of hydrogen and enhanced biosynthesis of hydrolases. More 
specifically, the negative charges on the surfaces of NBs could attract 
H+, which may be more easily reduced by NADH to H2 following 
NADH+H+→NAD++H2 (Cai et al., 2011). Tanisho et al. (1989) also 
found that the conversion of NADH to hydrogen could occur on the cell 
membranes, implying that the hydrogenase involved in the NADH 
pathway is a membrane-bound enzyme. Therefore, Air-NBs may pro­
mote the electron exchange between NADH ferredoxin oxidoreductase 
(NFOR) and hydrogenase to produce H2 due to it is negatively charged. 
For the methanogenesis stage, addition of Air-NBW also improves the 
activities of ETS and coenzyme F420, most probably attributable to its 
stimulation effect on electron transfer between bacteria and metha­
nogens. It also indirectly indicates that addition of Air-NBW enhanced 
microbial activity, resulting in increased CH4 production. Liu et al. 
(2015) and Xiao and Xu (2020) have verified that NBW could accelerate 
the metabolism of organisms, facilitating seed germination and biofilm 
growth. Still, more direct evidences are demanding for the above 
viewpoints in the followed-up works. 
4. Conclusions 
In this study, the hydrolysis/acidogenesis and methanogenesis stages 
were seriously inhibited at high salt levels (≥20 g NaCl/L). However, 
addition of Air-NBW reduced the inhibition of high salinity on the effi­
ciency of two-stage AD of FW, with hydrogen and methane yields 
increased by 21 – 65% and 14 – 43% in the Air-NBW added reactors in 
comparison to the DW added ones at 0 – 30 g NaCl/L. α-glucosidase and 
protease activities were enhanced by 9 – 20% and 0.4 – 22% at the end of 
the first stage, and coenzyme F420 activity was increased by 26 – 58% at 
the end of the second stage in the Air-NBW group with 0 – 30 g NaCl/L, 
respectively. Certainly, future works are necessary to emphasize the 
NBW application and performance in the large-scale and long-term
